stories.title: Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services
stories.summary: Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PQR9 Prefer DW on Google Cybercrime can also affect supermarkets, like Irish chain SuperValu whose cooling systems were hacked in early November Image: REUTERS Advertisement Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday. Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany. Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies. Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory". On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire. There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love." The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope. He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
